q: In goods traffic statistics, 'terminating traffic' of a railway means traffic which:

options.A: Both originates and terminates on the same railway
options.B: Terminates on that railway after having originated on another railway
options.C: Merely passes through that railway without originating or terminating on it
options.D: Is transhipped at a station of that railway en route

e: Terminating traffic is traffic received from another railway and ending on the home railway, as distinct from originating, local or through traffic in traffic statistics classification.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Fundamental statistics are the basic traffic units originally collected from the operating and commercial returns, such as tonnes, passengers, train kilometres and wagon kilometres.
2. Derived statistics are the ratios and averages worked out from the fundamental units, such as average lead, wagon turn-round and Net Tonne Kilometres per wagon day.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Fundamental statistics are the basic units collected from returns, like tonnes and train kilometres, while derived statistics are ratios and averages worked out from them, like average lead and wagon turn-round.

q: In railway operating statistics, 'train hours' represent:

options.A: The total time taken by trains in running from the starting station to the destination station, including detention en route
options.B: The total time for which locomotives remain inside the loco shed under repair
options.C: The total time spent by wagons in marshalling yards awaiting formation of trains
options.D: The total time taken in loading and unloading of wagons at terminals

e: Train hours mean the time from a train starting at its originating station to arrival at destination, including detentions en route, and are used with train kilometres for average speed.

q: The trailing gross load of a goods train, from which Gross Tonne Kilometres are worked out, is made up of:

options.A: The weight of the locomotive alone
options.B: The net weight of the goods carried alone
options.C: The tare weight of the wagons together with the net weight of the load carried in them
options.D: The carrying capacity marked on the wagons, whether loaded or empty

e: Gross Tonne Kilometres are based on trailing gross load, which is the tare weight of the wagons plus the net weight of the load carried in them, excluding the locomotive weight.

q: A parcel booked under the 'Value Payable Post' (VPP) system is delivered to the consignee:

options.A: Only after recovering from him the value of the article declared by the sender, which is then remitted to the sender
options.B: Free of all charges, the value being recovered later from the sender
options.C: Only against surrender of a separate bank guarantee for the declared value
options.D: Only at the booking station, after the sender confirms receipt of its value

e: Under the Value Payable Post system the parcel is delivered only after collecting the value declared by the sender from the consignee, and that value is then remitted to the sender.

q: Where only a part of a consignment booked under one Railway Receipt is delivered to the consignee at destination, the correct procedure is that:

options.A: The entire Railway Receipt is retained by the consignee without any endorsement
options.B: A fresh Railway Receipt is issued for the part delivered
options.C: The freight for the whole consignment is refunded at the time of part delivery
options.D: Part delivery is recorded on the Railway Receipt and a shortage certificate is issued for the portion not delivered

e: On part delivery, the delivery is endorsed on the Railway Receipt and a shortage certificate is issued for the undelivered portion, so the consignee can support a claim for the shortage.

q: In the charging of freight on a goods consignment, the 'chargeable distance' means:

options.A: The straight-line distance between the booking and destination stations
options.B: The distance over which the consignment is actually carried, computed in accordance with the prescribed rules, on which freight is charged
options.C: The route distance of the shortest passenger train between the two stations
options.D: The distance entered in the Forwarding Note by the consignor, without any check

e: Chargeable distance is the distance over which the consignment is actually carried, computed under the prescribed rules for charging freight, not a straight-line or unchecked declared distance.

q: For charging fares and freight over certain sections where the cost of working is exceptionally high, such as ghat sections, the distance used for charging is:

options.A: The actual distance of the section, without any addition
options.B: The distance of the longest alternative route
options.C: An inflated distance, that is, the actual distance increased in the prescribed manner
options.D: A notional distance fixed uniformly for all ghat sections of Indian Railways

e: On ghat and other high-cost sections, freight is charged on inflated distance, that is the actual distance increased in the prescribed manner, to reflect the higher cost of working.

q: A passenger holding a through journey ticket who wishes to break his journey at an intermediate station should, in his own interest:

options.A: Get the break of journey endorsed on his ticket by the station or ticket checking staff, as required under the rules
options.B: Simply retain the used portion of the ticket and resume the journey at any later date
options.C: Purchase a fresh ticket for the remaining portion and claim its refund afterwards
options.D: Hand over the ticket at the intermediate station and collect a duplicate on resuming the journey

e: A passenger breaking journey must get the break endorsed on the ticket by station or ticket checking staff, as required by the Commercial Manual rules, to prove authorised interruption.

q: In the Cash Office of a railway, the credits afforded by the bank for the remittances made by stations are reconciled primarily with the help of:

options.A: The collected tickets received from the stations
options.B: The bank scrolls received from the bank, compared with the remittance particulars rendered by the stations
options.C: The goods invoices rendered by the forwarding stations
options.D: The monthly evaluation report of earnings

e: Bank credits for station remittances are reconciled in the Cash Office by comparing bank scrolls with the remittance particulars rendered by stations, matching each credit to its remittance.

q: Tickets which are spoiled or rendered defective at a station before issue, for example by wrong printing or wrong entry, are dealt with by the station by:

options.A: Destroying them at the station itself without any record
options.B: Issuing them to passengers at a reduced fare
options.C: Treating them as non-issued tickets without any separate accountal
options.D: Cancelling them, keeping them on record and rendering them to the Traffic Accounts Office with the station accounts

e: Tickets spoiled before issue are non-issued tickets: they are cancelled, retained on record and rendered to the Traffic Accounts Office with the station accounts for accountal and check.

q: Perishable consignments lying undelivered at a destination station are dealt with on a priority basis, and where they remain unclaimed, because:

options.A: Delay in their disposal results in deterioration and loss, so they are disposed of promptly in accordance with the rules instead of being held like ordinary goods
options.B: Perishable goods can never be auctioned under the Railways Act
options.C: The Railways do not levy wharfage on perishable goods in any circumstances
options.D: Perishable goods are returned to the booking station at railway cost in every case

e: Perishables deteriorate quickly, so unclaimed perishables are disposed of promptly on priority under the rules and Section 85 of the Railways Act, instead of being held like ordinary goods.

q: Where live stock is booked for carriage by rail, the arrangements for feeding and watering the animals during the journey and for an attendant to accompany them are, under the rules, primarily the responsibility of:

options.A: The destination station staff
options.B: The Traffic Accounts Office
options.C: The consignor
options.D: The train guard, as part of his normal duties

e: For livestock booked by rail, feeding, watering and providing an attendant during transit are primarily the consignor's responsibility under the goods booking rules, not the Railways'.

q: Freight on a goods consignment is subject to a prescribed minimum charge, which means that:

options.A: Freight is waived altogether if the charge worked out is below the minimum
options.B: Where the freight worked out at the applicable rate is less than the prescribed minimum, the minimum charge is recovered
options.C: The minimum charge is recovered in addition to the freight worked out at the applicable rate
options.D: The minimum charge applies only to traffic booked at owner's risk

e: A minimum charge means that if freight worked out at the applicable rate is below the prescribed minimum, the minimum charge itself is recovered for the consignment.

q: 'Assessment delivery' of a consignment at destination, as distinguished from 'open delivery', refers to delivery granted:

options.A: Without production of the Railway Receipt, on execution of an indemnity bond
options.B: After opening the packages and examining their contents in the presence of the consignee
options.C: Only on the orders of the Railway Claims Tribunal
options.D: After the damage or deficiency in the consignment has been assessed by the competent railway official and recorded, where the consignee seeks delivery on that basis

e: Assessment delivery is delivery granted after the damage or deficiency is assessed by the competent railway official and recorded, where the consignee seeks delivery on that assessed basis.

q: A 'General Indemnity Bond' in connection with delivery of goods is a bond executed by a consignee who:

options.A: Regularly takes delivery of consignments without production of the original Railway Receipt, the bond covering such deliveries generally instead of a separate bond on each occasion
options.B: Desires to book goods at railway risk instead of owner's risk
options.C: Claims a refund of freight on a consignment already delivered
options.D: Registers a demand for supply of wagons at a station

e: A General Indemnity Bond covers a regular consignee generally for taking delivery without production of the original Railway Receipt on each occasion, instead of a separate bond every time.

q: The duties of a Commercial Inspector on a railway include, among other things:

options.A: Compilation of the Accounts Office Balance Sheet in the Traffic Accounts Office
options.B: Inspection of stations and goods sheds in his beat to see that traffic is booked and accounted for correctly and that there is no leakage of revenue
options.C: Apportionment of through earnings among the zonal railways
options.D: Conduct of the statutory audit of station accounts on behalf of the Audit Office

e: A Commercial Inspector inspects stations and goods sheds in his beat to see that traffic is correctly booked and accounted for and that there is no leakage of railway revenue.

q: The daily interchange of wagons at junctions between two zonal railways is important for traffic accounts and statistics mainly because it enables each railway to work out its:

options.A: Coaching earnings for the day
options.B: Passenger classification for the month
options.C: Daily wagon balance, that is, the wagon stock position on its system after wagons handed over and received are taken into account
options.D: Specific Fuel Consumption for the day

e: Daily wagon interchange at junctions lets each railway arrive at its daily wagon balance, that is its wagon stock after adding wagons received and deducting wagons handed over.

q: Wagons described as 'non-pooled' wagons are wagons which:

options.A: Are owned by private wagon owners under an investment scheme
options.B: Have been declared as dead surplus by the owning railway
options.C: Are used exclusively for departmental traffic of the home railway
options.D: Are not thrown into the common wagon pool and are required to be returned to the owning railway after unloading

e: Non-pooled wagons are not thrown into the common wagon pool; they must be returned to the owning railway after unloading, unlike pooled wagons used freely by any railway.

q: In wagon utilisation statistics, 'terminal detention' of a wagon refers to:

options.A: The time for which a wagon is detained at the loading and unloading terminals for the operations of loading and unloading
options.B: The time taken by a wagon in running between two marshalling yards
options.C: The time for which a wagon remains under repair in a workshop
options.D: The time spent by a wagon in a loco shed awaiting a locomotive

e: Terminal detention is the time a wagon is detained at loading and unloading terminals for those operations, as distinct from running time or yard and repair detention.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Detention of wagons in marshalling yards, while trains are being formed and re-formed, forms part of the total time taken in the wagon turn-round.
2. Reducing detention at terminals and in marshalling yards is one of the ways of improving the wagon turn-round.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Yard detention during formation and re-formation of trains forms part of wagon turn-round, so reducing detention at terminals and yards directly improves the turn-round figure.

q: 'Tonnes carried' in goods traffic statistics differ from 'tonnes originating' mainly in that tonnes carried:

options.A: Include only the traffic booked at owner's risk
options.B: Take into account the tonnes handled at each stage of the movement, so that through traffic is counted by every railway which carries it, whereas tonnes originating are counted once, by the railway on which the traffic originates
options.C: Are always less than the tonnes originating on a railway
options.D: Exclude all traffic received from foreign railways for delivery

e: Tonnes carried count traffic at each carrying stage, so every railway carrying through traffic counts it, whereas tonnes originating are counted once only by the originating railway.

q: In coaching statistics, 'vehicles in use' on a day means the coaching vehicles which are:

options.A: Standing in the coaching yard awaiting cleaning and examination
options.B: Under repair or awaiting repair in sick lines and workshops
options.C: Kept as a spare margin for emergencies and not run in trains
options.D: Actually employed in running trains during the day, as distinct from the total vehicles on line

e: Vehicles in use are coaching vehicles actually employed in running trains during the day, as distinct from the total vehicles on line including spare, sick and yard vehicles.

q: 'Stacking' of goods at a goods shed, for which permission of the competent station authority is obtained, refers to:

options.A: Allowing the consignor or consignee to keep the goods stacked in the goods shed or station premises for a period beyond the time allowed for loading or removal, on the conditions and charges prescribed
options.B: Loading of goods in a wagon in layers so as to exceed its marked carrying capacity
options.C: Keeping of unclaimed goods in a separate godown after public auction
options.D: Arrangement of packages inside a parcel van in the order of destination stations

e: Stacking is permission to keep goods stacked in the goods shed or station premises beyond the free time for loading or removal, on the prescribed conditions and charges.

q: Booking of goods traffic to a particular destination is sometimes temporarily restricted by the Railways. Such booking restrictions are imposed mainly:

options.A: To increase the freight earnings from that destination
options.B: By the operating authorities when congestion, congestion at the destination terminal or other operating conditions make it necessary to regulate the flow of traffic
options.C: By the Traffic Accounts Office when station outstandings at that station are heavy
options.D: At the request of the consignees at the destination station

e: Booking restrictions are imposed by operating authorities to regulate traffic flow when congestion at destination or other operating conditions make unrestricted booking impracticable.

q: Earnings which have accrued to a station during a month but have not actually been collected by the close of the month are shown in the station accounts as:

options.A: Sundry earnings of the following month
options.B: A loss to be written off by the station
options.C: Outstandings in the Station Balance Sheet, to be cleared on their actual realisation
options.D: An item of Traffic Suspense in the general books directly, without passing through the station accounts

e: Earnings accrued but not collected by month-end are shown as outstandings in the Station Balance Sheet, and are cleared later when the amounts are actually realised.

q: Cash remitted by a station to the Cash Office or bank is normally sent:

options.A: In loose bundles accompanied by the station balance sheet of the month
options.B: Through the guard of a passenger train without any document
options.C: By deducting it from the earnings of the following day, without any remittance note
options.D: In a sealed cash bag, accompanied by a remittance note showing the amount remitted

e: Station cash is remitted in a sealed cash bag accompanied by a remittance note showing the amount, so the Cash Office or bank can identify and account for the remittance.

q: When a station master is relieved of his charge by another official, the cash, tickets and other accountable forms of the station are taken over in a manner which ensures that:

options.A: The relieving official takes over charge only after a joint check of the cash, ticket stock and records, and the taking over is recorded and signed for
options.B: The relieved official carries the ticket stock with him to his next station
options.C: The station earnings of the day of relief are shared between the two officials
options.D: No record of the taking over is necessary if both officials belong to the same station

e: On relief, the relieving official takes over cash, tickets and accountable forms only after a joint check, with the taking over recorded and signed, fixing responsibility for the stock.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. An overcharge detected in the Traffic Accounts Office check is advised through an overcharge sheet so that the amount can be refunded to the party entitled, without the party being required to prefer a formal claim for it.
2. An undercharge detected in the check is recovered from the party liable through the station accounts.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Overcharges detected in Traffic Accounts check are refunded through an overcharge sheet without a formal claim, while undercharges are recovered from the liable party through station accounts.

q: Bulk consignments such as coal and ores loaded in wagons are weighed for the purpose of charging freight, and the result of such weighment is recorded:

options.A: Only in the private diary of the goods clerk
options.B: On the invoice and the Railway Receipt, so that freight is charged on the weight so recorded, subject to the rules for chargeable weight
options.C: Only in the loco shed return of the forwarding station
options.D: In the passenger classification return of the forwarding station

e: For bulk wagonload traffic like coal and ores, the weighment result is recorded on the invoice and Railway Receipt, and freight is charged on that recorded chargeable weight.

q: The statistics of fuel and energy consumption of locomotives on a zonal railway are compiled primarily from:

options.A: The returns rendered by the loco sheds and depots showing the fuel and energy drawn and consumed by locomotives
options.B: The goods invoices rendered by the forwarding stations
options.C: The collected tickets received from stations
options.D: The siding statements rendered by stations having private sidings

e: Locomotive fuel and energy statistics are compiled from loco shed and depot returns showing fuel and energy drawn and consumed, which are the primary records of consumption.

q: The total cost of coaching services of a railway for a period is Rs 60,00,000 and the passenger kilometres performed are 30,00,000. The cost per passenger kilometre works out to:
e: Cost per passenger kilometre is total cost divided by passenger kilometres: Rs 60,00,000 divided by 30,00,000 passenger kilometres gives Rs 2.00 per passenger kilometre.

q: One 'wagon day' in goods statistics is equivalent to:

options.A: One wagon remaining loaded for one complete loaded trip
options.B: One wagon running 100 kilometres in a day
options.C: One wagon loaded and unloaded once on the same day
options.D: Twenty-four wagon-hours, that is, the availability or use of one wagon for a period of twenty-four hours

e: One wagon day equals 24 wagon-hours, that is the availability or use of one wagon for 24 hours, and is the denominator unit for Net Tonne Kilometres per wagon day.

q: Where a consignment loaded in an open wagon requires protection against weather during transit, it is covered with tarpaulins, and:

options.A: Tarpaulins are never supplied by the Railways in any circumstances
options.B: The cost of the tarpaulins so used is borne entirely by the destination station
options.C: The consignment is refused booking unless it is transferred to a covered wagon
options.D: Tarpaulin hire or covering charges, where prescribed, are recovered from the party concerned in addition to the freight

e: Consignments in open wagons needing weather protection are covered with tarpaulins, and tarpaulin hire or covering charges, where prescribed, are recovered from the party besides freight.

q: Before a consignment is accepted for booking, each package is required to bear clear marks and labels indicating the consignor, the consignee and the destination station, mainly in order to:

options.A: Identify the packages during transit and at destination and to prevent their going astray or being delivered wrongly
options.B: Enable the Railways to levy a separate marking charge on every package
options.C: Decide the class rate applicable to the commodity booked
options.D: Fix the free time admissible for unloading at the destination

e: Marks and labels showing consignor, consignee and destination identify each package in transit and at destination, preventing packages going astray or being wrongly delivered.

q: Under Section 105 of the Railways Act, 1989, where the value of a consignment has been declared under Section 103, the railway administration may, in order to verify that the consignment contains the articles declared:

options.A: Refuse the consignment and forfeit the freight already paid
options.B: Demand production of the consignment and examine its contents for verification, in accordance with the provisions of the Act
options.C: Levy demurrage on the consignment until the consignor files a claim
options.D: Auction the consignment forthwith without notice to the consignor

e: Section 105 of the Railways Act gives the railway the right to check contents of a consignment by examination by an authorised servant, to verify that it contains the articles declared.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Under Section 99 of the Railways Act, 1989, after the termination of the transit of a consignment, the railway administration continues to be responsible for it, in the capacity of a bailee, for the period and on the conditions provided in that section.
2. The responsibility of the railway administration for a consignment during its transit is dealt with in Section 93 of the Railways Act, 1989.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Section 93 lays down the railway's general responsibility as carrier during transit, and Section 99 continues its responsibility as bailee after termination of transit, so both statements hold.

q: Under the Railways Act, 1989, a claim for refund of fare or freight, or for compensation, can be preferred by:

options.A: Any passenger who happens to travel by the same train
options.B: The station master of the destination station on his own behalf
options.C: Only the railway employee who issued the ticket or the Railway Receipt
options.D: The person entitled to claim it, that is, the party on whom the right to the refund or compensation rests under the Act and the rules

e: Under the Railways Act a refund or compensation can be claimed only by the person entitled to it, that is the party on whom the right rests, as in Section 108 for compensation.

q: Drunkenness or nuisance committed by a person in a railway carriage or on railway premises, and failure to leave a carriage when requested on that account, is an offence dealt with under the Railways Act, 1989 in:

options.A: Section 145
options.B: Section 106
options.C: Section 93
options.D: Section 123

e: Drunkenness or nuisance in a carriage or on railway premises, and refusing to leave when requested, is an offence under Section 145 of the Railways Act, 1989.

q: A person who obstructs or impedes a railway servant in the discharge of his duties commits an offence under the Railways Act, 1989 dealt with in:

options.A: Section 99
options.B: Section 146
options.C: Section 105
options.D: Section 137

e: Obstructing or impeding a railway servant in the discharge of his duties is an offence under Section 146 of the Railways Act, 1989.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Revenue-earning Net Tonne Kilometres cover the traffic carried for the public for hire or reward.
2. Departmental traffic carried for the Railways' own use, which does not yield traffic earnings, is not counted as revenue-earning traffic in the earnings statistics.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Revenue-earning Net Tonne Kilometres cover only public traffic carried for hire or reward; departmental traffic for the Railways' own use yields no earnings and is excluded from them.

q: Kilometres run by an engine in shunting at stations and yards are classified in operating statistics as:

options.A: Train kilometres, in the same way as kilometres run with trains on the open line
options.B: Coaching vehicle kilometres of the trains shunted
options.C: Nil, since shunting movements are excluded from all operating statistics
options.D: Engine kilometres under the shunting head, and not as train kilometres

e: Engine kilometres run in shunting are counted as engine kilometres under the shunting head, not as train kilometres, which cover only kilometres run with trains on the open line.

q: For compiling the ten-day statement of approximate gross earnings, the figures of earnings collected at stations reach the compiling office through:

options.A: The daily advices or returns of earnings rendered by the stations and divisions for the period
options.B: The audited Appropriation Accounts of the previous year
options.C: The overcharge sheets issued by the Traffic Accounts Office
options.D: The stock verification sheets of the Accounts Department

e: The ten-day approximate gross earnings statement is compiled from the daily advices and returns of earnings rendered by stations and divisions for the ten-day period.

q: Where freight on a wagonload consignment is charged on the basis of the carrying capacity of the wagon used, the weight charged for is:

options.A: The actual net weight of the goods found on weighment, in all cases
options.B: The minimum chargeable weight prescribed for the wagon or the class of traffic, even if the actual weight loaded is less
options.C: The tare weight of the wagon supplied for loading
options.D: The weight declared by the consignor in the Forwarding Note, without reference to the wagon capacity

e: Where wagonload freight is charged on wagon capacity, the minimum chargeable weight prescribed for the wagon or class applies even if the actual weight loaded is less than it.

q: After an inspection of a station is completed, the Travelling Inspector of Accounts:

options.A: Closes the station accounts finally and signs the Station Balance Sheet himself
options.B: Submits an inspection report bringing out the irregularities noticed, which are pursued with the station and the executive authorities for rectification and for clearance of the outstandings
options.C: Writes off all the debits outstanding against the station at the time of inspection
options.D: Takes over the charge of the station from the station master for the following month

e: After inspecting a station, the Travelling Inspector of Accounts submits an inspection report of irregularities, which is pursued with the station and executives for rectification.

q: In goods and coaching traffic statistics, traffic which both originates and terminates on the same railway, without passing over any other railway, is classified as:

options.A: Local traffic of that railway
options.B: Through traffic of that railway
options.C: Foreign traffic of that railway
options.D: Transhipment traffic of that railway

e: Traffic which both originates and terminates on the same railway, without passing over any other railway, is by definition local traffic of that railway.

q: The traffic earnings brought to account by a railway for a month differ from the cash actually collected at its stations during the month mainly because earnings are accounted for:

options.A: Only when the cash is received in the Cash Office
options.B: On the accrual basis, that is, for the traffic booked and the services rendered during the month, whether the amount has been collected in cash or is still to be realised
options.C: Only for the traffic for which the Railway Receipts have been surrendered
options.D: On the basis of the bank scrolls alone, without reference to the traffic booked

e: Traffic earnings are accounted on the accrual basis for traffic booked and services rendered in the month, whether collected in cash or still realisable, not on cash collection alone.

q: In goods traffic statistics, 'transhipped traffic' at a station refers to traffic which is:

options.A: Booked at that station for a destination on the same railway
options.B: Delivered at that station after originating on another railway
options.C: Unloaded from one wagon and loaded into another wagon at that station en route, as at a break-of-gauge point, for onward carriage to its destination
options.D: Carried past that station without any stoppage

e: Transhipped traffic is unloaded from one wagon and loaded into another at a station en route, as at a break-of-gauge point, for onward carriage to its destination.

q: The Net Tonne Kilometres performed on a railway during a period are 27,50,000 and the wagon days during the same period are 55,000. The Net Tonne Kilometres per wagon day work out to:
e: Net Tonne Kilometres per wagon day is 27,50,000 divided by 55,000 wagon days, which works out to 50, the standard measure of wagon productivity.

q: The Net Tonne Kilometres performed on a railway during a period are 96,00,000 and the tonnes carried during the same period are 1,20,000. The average lead of the goods traffic works out to:

options.A: 60 kilometres
options.B: 80 kilometres
options.C: 100 kilometres
options.D: 120 kilometres

e: Average lead is Net Tonne Kilometres divided by tonnes carried: 96,00,000 divided by 1,20,000 tonnes gives an average lead of 80 kilometres.

q: The gross earnings of a railway for a year are Rs 4,000 crore and its working expenses for the year are Rs 3,400 crore. The Operating Ratio of the railway for the year works out to:

options.A: 85 per cent
options.B: 90 per cent
options.C: 80 per cent
options.D: 75 per cent

e: Operating Ratio is working expenses as a percentage of gross earnings: Rs 3,400 crore divided by Rs 4,000 crore and multiplied by 100 gives 85 per cent.

q: During a month, the total wagon days on a railway were 8,40,000 and the number of wagons loaded during the month was 2,10,000. The wagon turn-round for the month works out to:

options.A: 2 days
options.B: 3 days
options.C: 5 days
options.D: 4 days

e: Wagon turn-round is wagon days divided by wagons loaded: 8,40,000 divided by 2,10,000 gives 4 days, the average time taken for a wagon to complete its cycle.

q: The total cost of the coaching services of a railway for a period is Rs 45,00,000 and the passenger kilometres performed during the period are 90,00,000. The cost per passenger kilometre works out to:
e: Cost per passenger kilometre is Rs 45,00,000 divided by 90,00,000 passenger kilometres, which works out to Rs 0.50 per passenger kilometre.

q: A consignment is unloaded from the wagon within the free time allowed, but the consignee does not remove it from the station premises within the free time allowed for removal. The charge that accrues in this case for the period beyond the free time is:

options.A: Demurrage, because the wagon was detained
options.B: Siding charges, because the goods were kept in a siding
options.C: Stabling charges, because the goods were kept at the station
options.D: Wharfage, because the goods were allowed to lie at the station premises beyond the free time after unloading

e: Wharfage is charged when goods, though unloaded within free time, are not removed from station premises within the free removal time; demurrage applies only to wagon detention.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Demurrage accrues when a wagon is detained beyond the free time allowed for its loading or unloading.
2. Wharfage accrues when goods are not removed from the station premises within the free time allowed after their unloading.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: By definition demurrage accrues for detaining a wagon beyond free time for loading or unloading, and wharfage for not removing goods from station premises within free time after unloading.

q: The siding statements rendered by stations having private or assisted sidings are checked in the Traffic Accounts Office mainly to ensure that:

options.A: The siding charges and the charges for placement and removal of wagons due from the siding owners are correctly levied and brought to account
options.B: The pay of the siding staff is correctly drawn
options.C: The wagons owned by the siding owners are repaired in time
options.D: The commodities dealt with at the sidings are correctly classified for statistics

e: Siding statements are checked in the Traffic Accounts Office to ensure siding charges and placement and removal charges due from siding owners are correctly levied and accounted.

q: Loaded wagons despatched from a station are sealed, and the numbers of the seals are recorded on the seal card and allied documents, mainly in order to:

options.A: Decide the class rate applicable to the goods loaded in the wagon
options.B: Work out the tare weight of the wagon for charging freight
options.C: Fix the free time admissible for unloading at the destination
options.D: Enable the seals to be checked at the destination and at interchange points, so that any interference with the wagon en route can be detected

e: Seals on loaded wagons and their numbers on seal cards let seals be checked at destination and interchange points, so any interference with the wagon en route is detected.

q: Where the railway administration has reason to suspect that the weight of a consignment in transit has been incorrectly declared, the consignment may be subjected to:

options.A: Auction at the next station without notice to the consignor
options.B: Weighment en route or at destination by the Railways, and freight may be re-assessed on the weight so found in accordance with the rules
options.C: Forfeiture of the freight already paid, in every case
options.D: Delivery only against a fresh Forwarding Note from the consignor

e: If weight is suspected to be wrongly declared, the Railways may weigh the consignment en route or at destination and re-assess freight on the weight found, under the weighment rules.

q: Every loaded wagon despatched from a station bears a wagon label showing, among other particulars, the destination station and the particulars of the load, mainly in order to:

options.A: Enable the wagon to be correctly marshalled, despatched and delivered to its destination during transit
options.B: Serve as a receipt for the freight paid by the consignor
options.C: Replace the Railway Receipt for the consignment loaded in the wagon
options.D: Record the earnings collected at the forwarding station

e: The wagon label showing destination and load particulars enables the wagon to be correctly marshalled, despatched and delivered during transit to its proper destination.

q: As distinguished from a parcel, 'luggage' in railway working means:

options.A: Any goods consignment booked on a Parcel Way Bill and carried in a brake van
options.B: The goods carried for the Post Office under a mail contract
options.C: The parcels offered by a trader for carriage to his customers
options.D: The personal effects and belongings of a passenger, carried in connection with his own journey and booked on a luggage ticket

e: Luggage means a passenger's personal effects carried in connection with his own journey and booked on a luggage ticket, unlike parcels booked on a Parcel Way Bill for others.

q: The amounts received by the Railways from the Post Office for the carriage of mails and postal vehicles by trains are classified in the railway accounts under:

options.A: Goods earnings
options.B: Passenger earnings proper
options.C: Other coaching earnings
options.D: Sundry other earnings

e: Amounts received from the Post Office for carriage of mails and postal vehicles are classified as other coaching earnings, not passenger, goods or sundry earnings.

q: At the close of a financial year, the Finance branch of a zonal railway insists that the items lying under Traffic Suspense be cleared to the maximum extent before the accounts of the year are closed, mainly because:

options.A: Uncleared Traffic Suspense items earn interest for the railway
options.B: Traffic Suspense items are transferred to the Capital account at the year end
options.C: The station staff are transferred at the close of every financial year
options.D: Amounts recoverable for traffic services which remain unrealised and unadjusted distort the earnings and the financial results, including the Operating Ratio, of the year

e: Uncleared Traffic Suspense items are recoverable traffic amounts left unrealised; they distort earnings and the Operating Ratio, so Finance insists on maximum clearance before year close.

q: The Accounts Office Balance Sheet in traffic accounts differs from the Station Balance Sheet mainly in that the Accounts Office Balance Sheet:

options.A: Is prepared by the station master for his own station alone
options.B: Shows only the coaching earnings of the railway
options.C: Is a substitute for the monthly evaluation report of earnings
options.D: Consolidates the balances of the stations with the adjustments and debits advised by the Traffic Accounts Office after its check of the station accounts

e: The Accounts Office Balance Sheet consolidates station balances with the adjustments and debits advised by the Traffic Accounts Office after its check, unlike a single station's balance sheet.

q: Kilometres run by an additional engine which assists a train engine in hauling a train, for example a banking engine on a ghat section, are classified in operating statistics as:

options.A: Train kilometres of an additional train
options.B: Assisted engine kilometres, counted as engine kilometres but not as train kilometres
options.C: Coaching vehicle kilometres of the train assisted
options.D: Light engine kilometres in every case

e: Kilometres of an assisting or banking engine are assisted engine kilometres, counted as engine kilometres but not as train kilometres, since only one train is run.

q: The time spent by engines in shunting wagons and vehicles at stations and in yards is accounted for in operating statistics:

options.A: As train hours of the trains formed by that shunting
options.B: As coaching hours of the vehicles shunted
options.C: Separately as shunting engine time, and not as train hours of trains run on the open line
options.D: It is excluded from all operating statistics altogether

e: Time engines spend shunting wagons and vehicles at stations and yards is accounted separately as shunting engine time, not as train hours of trains on the open line.

q: For deciding whether a particular traffic can be carried at a proposed concessional rate, the traffic costing organisation furnishes, among other things, the cost which is directly attributable to that traffic, because pricing decisions are judged mainly against:

options.A: The specific or avoidable cost of carrying that traffic, together with its contribution to the common costs
options.B: The total capital-at-charge of the railway
options.C: The pay and allowances of the commercial staff alone
options.D: The earnings of the highest-earning commodity of the railway

e: For judging a concessional rate, costing furnishes the specific or avoidable cost of that traffic, since pricing is judged against that cost and its contribution to common costs.

q: Under the principle commonly described as charging 'what the traffic can bear', the classification of commodities for freight rating is so arranged that, broadly:

options.A: All commodities are charged at one uniform rate per kilometre
options.B: The rate depends only on the tare weight of the wagon used
options.C: Bulk traffic of low value is charged at the highest class rate
options.D: Articles of high value, which can bear a higher charge, are placed in higher classes, while low-value bulk commodities are placed in lower classes

e: Charging what the traffic can bear places high-value articles that can bear higher charges in higher classes and low-value bulk commodities in lower classes for freight rating.

q: Licence fees and rents received by a railway for the hoardings and advertisement boards displayed at stations and on railway land are classified in the railway accounts under:

options.A: Passenger earnings
options.B: Goods earnings
options.C: Sundry other earnings
options.D: Other coaching earnings

e: Licence fees and rents for hoardings and advertisement boards at stations and on railway land are sundry other earnings, not passenger, goods or other coaching earnings.

q: Under Section 103 of the Railways Act, 1989, where the consignor declares the value of the consignment and pays the prescribed percentage charge on that value, the monetary liability of the railway administration for loss of or damage to the consignment is, broadly:

options.A: Unlimited, irrespective of the value declared
options.B: Limited to the value so declared by the consignor
options.C: Limited to the freight paid on the consignment alone
options.D: Nil, because the percentage charge is paid by the consignor

e: Under Section 103 of the Railways Act, where value is declared and the prescribed percentage charge is paid, the railway's monetary liability is limited to the value so declared.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. An ex gratia payment made to the victims of a train accident is an immediate relief payment and does not by itself amount to the compensation payable under the Railways Act.
2. The ex gratia amount so paid is adjusted against the compensation finally awarded to the claimant for the same accident.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: Both 1 and 2
options.B: 1 only
options.C: 2 only
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Ex gratia is only immediate relief and is not itself Act compensation, and for train accidents and untoward incidents it is not taken into account against the final compensation, so only statement 1 holds.

q: A freight customer who has booked a consignment is able to follow the movement of his wagon or consignment after booking mainly through:

options.A: The station balance sheet of the forwarding station
options.B: The overcharge sheets issued by the Traffic Accounts Office
options.C: The stock verification reports of the Accounts Department
options.D: The wagon and consignment tracing facilities built on the data captured in the Freight Operations Information System

e: A freight customer traces his wagon or consignment through the tracing facilities built on data captured in the Freight Operations Information System, FOIS.

q: The wharfage and demurrage returns rendered by stations are checked in the Traffic Accounts Office mainly to ensure that:

options.A: The wagons detained at the stations are repaired promptly
options.B: The charges have been levied in accordance with the rules, and remissions, where allowed, are only those sanctioned by the competent authority
options.C: The goods sheds are kept open for the prescribed hours
options.D: The siding owners have paid their licence fees in time

e: Wharfage and demurrage returns are checked to ensure charges were levied under the rules and that remissions are only those sanctioned by the competent authority.

q: The handling bills rendered by stations are checked in the Traffic Accounts Office mainly to ensure that:

options.A: The handling contractors have engaged the prescribed number of labourers
options.B: The wagons handled at the station are owned by the home railway
options.C: The payments claimed for the loading, unloading or transhipment work relate to the traffic actually handled and are in accordance with the sanctioned rates and contracts
options.D: The goods handled at the station are insured by the parties

e: Handling bills are checked to ensure payments claimed for loading, unloading or transhipment relate to traffic actually handled and are at the sanctioned rates and contract terms.

q: A station master proposes to meet an urgent payment due to a handling contractor at his station directly out of the earnings collected at the station, and to remit only the balance to the Cash Office. The correct position is that:

options.A: Station earnings are required to be remitted in full, and payments on behalf of the Railways are not to be made by appropriating the earnings collected at the station except under proper authority and through the prescribed accountal
options.B: The proposal is in order, since the net amount reaching the Railways remains the same
options.C: The proposal is in order only for coaching earnings, and not for goods earnings
options.D: The proposal is in order if the amount involved is small

e: Station earnings must be remitted in full; a station cannot appropriate collections for payments on behalf of the Railways except under proper authority and prescribed accountal.

q: The remittance note which accompanies the cash remitted by a station to the Cash Office or bank serves mainly to:

options.A: Replace the Station Balance Sheet for the month
options.B: Authorise the station master to retain a part of the earnings at the station
options.C: Identify the remittance with the station and the date to which it relates, so that the corresponding credit can be accounted for and reconciled in the Cash Office
options.D: Record the tickets issued by the station on the day of remittance

e: The remittance note identifies the remittance with the station and date, so the Cash Office can account for the corresponding bank credit and reconcile it correctly.

q: Goods freight rates on Indian Railways are framed on a telescopic or tapering basis, which broadly means that:

options.A: The rate per kilometre increases uniformly with every additional kilometre of carriage
options.B: The rate per kilometre decreases as the distance of carriage increases, so that long-distance traffic is charged at a lower rate per kilometre than short-distance traffic
options.C: One flat rate is charged irrespective of the distance of carriage
options.D: The rate depends only on the number of wagons in the train

e: Telescopic or tapering freight rates mean the rate per kilometre falls as distance increases, so long-distance traffic pays a lower rate per kilometre than short-distance traffic.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The average lead of goods traffic is also referred to as the average haul of the traffic.
2. The average lead is worked out by dividing the Net Tonne Kilometres performed by the tonnes carried.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Average lead, also called average haul, is Net Tonne Kilometres divided by tonnes carried, so both statements correctly state the same operating statistic and its formula.

q: The Gross Tonne Kilometres performed on a railway during a period are 1,20,00,000 and the engine days during the same period are 40,000. The Gross Tonne Kilometres per engine day work out to:
e: Gross Tonne Kilometres per engine day is 1,20,00,000 divided by 40,000 engine days, which works out to 300.

q: The working expenses of a railway for a period are Rs 72,00,000 and the train kilometres performed during the period are 24,00,000. The working expenses per train kilometre work out to:
e: Working expenses per train kilometre is Rs 72,00,000 divided by 24,00,000 train kilometres, which works out to Rs 3.00 per train kilometre.

q: A section of a railway is 500 route kilometres long and the Net Tonne Kilometres performed on the section during a period are 50,00,000. The density of goods traffic on the section, expressed as Net Tonne Kilometres per route kilometre, works out to:
e: Traffic density is Net Tonne Kilometres divided by route kilometres: 50,00,000 divided by 500 gives 10,000 Net Tonne Kilometres per route kilometre.

q: The Net Tonne Kilometres performed on a railway during a period are 36,00,000 and the available tonne kilometres offered during the same period are 60,00,000. The utilisation of the goods carrying capacity offered works out to:

options.A: 40 per cent
options.B: 60 per cent
options.C: 50 per cent
options.D: 75 per cent

e: Utilisation of carrying capacity is Net Tonne Kilometres divided by available tonne kilometres: 36,00,000 divided by 60,00,000 gives 60 per cent.

q: The passenger kilometres performed by the coaching services of a railway during a period are 7,20,000 and the seat kilometres offered during the same period are 9,00,000. The load factor of the coaching services works out to:

options.A: 80 per cent
options.B: 70 per cent
options.C: 60 per cent
options.D: 90 per cent

e: Load factor is passenger kilometres divided by seat kilometres offered: 7,20,000 divided by 9,00,000 gives a load factor of 80 per cent.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Freight on a consignment booked on the 'paid' basis is accounted for by the forwarding station which collects it at the time of booking.
2. Freight on a consignment booked on the 'to-pay' basis is accounted for by the destination station which recovers it at the time of delivery.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Paid freight is collected and accounted by the forwarding station at booking, while to-pay freight is recovered and accounted by the destination station at delivery, so both hold.

q: In the apportionment of the earnings of through goods traffic among the railways which carried it, after the share for the terminal services is set apart, the balance of the earnings is apportioned among the railways mainly on the basis of:

options.A: The number of wagons owned by each railway
options.B: The distance over which each railway carried the traffic
options.C: The number of stations situated on each railway
options.D: The staff strength of the commercial department of each railway

e: In apportionment of through goods earnings, after setting apart the terminal share, the balance is divided among carrying railways mainly in proportion to distance carried by each.

q: A party which books a complete coach or tourist car for a special journey on payment of the prescribed charges at the full tariff rate is availing of the facility generally known as booking on:

options.A: Concession rate
options.B: Military warrant
options.C: Indemnity bond
options.D: Full Tariff Rate (FTR)

e: Booking a complete coach or tourist car at the full prescribed tariff charges is booking on Full Tariff Rate, known as FTR, not a concession, warrant or indemnity facility.

q: Where a wagon is found on weighment to have been loaded beyond its permissible carrying capacity, the excess load is dealt with, in accordance with the rules, broadly by:

options.A: Adjusting or off-loading the excess load and dealing with it separately, with the charges leviable for the overloading being recovered as prescribed
options.B: Allowing the wagon to proceed to its destination in every case without any adjustment
options.C: Auctioning the entire consignment at the weighment station
options.D: Refunding the freight for the whole consignment to the consignor

e: A wagon loaded beyond permissible carrying capacity has the excess adjusted or off-loaded and dealt with separately, with the prescribed overloading charges recovered.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Engine kilometres per engine day 'in use' are worked out with reference only to the days on which the engines were actually in use.
2. Engine kilometres per engine day 'on line' are worked out with reference to all the engine days on line, including the days on which the engines were not in use.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Engine kilometres per engine day in use use only days engines were actually in use, while per engine day on line use all engine days on line including idle days, so both hold.

q: Even after the availability of operating data through systems such as FOIS, PRS and UTS, the ten-day statement of approximate gross earnings continues to be compiled mainly because it:

options.A: Replaces the final monthly earnings for the purposes of the annual accounts
options.B: Is the basis on which fares and freight rates are revised every ten days
options.C: Is used for the apportionment of earnings among the zonal railways
options.D: Provides a quick official appraisal of the trend of earnings for the Railway Board and the zonal railways, well before the final monthly figures are brought to account

e: The ten-day approximate earnings statement gives the Railway Board and zones a quick official appraisal of the earnings trend well before final monthly figures are accounted.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Net Tonne Kilometres worked out for revenue-earning traffic cover only the traffic carried for the public.
2. Net Tonne Kilometres of departmental traffic, carried for the Railways' own use, are not counted in the revenue-earning Net Tonne Kilometres.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Revenue-earning Net Tonne Kilometres cover only public traffic; departmental traffic for the Railways' own use is excluded from revenue-earning Net Tonne Kilometres, so both hold.

q: For the purposes of coaching earnings and passenger statistics, the passenger earnings of a railway are broadly classified into suburban and non-suburban earnings, the suburban earnings being those relating to:

options.A: The local and commuter services, such as the EMU and local train services, run in the notified suburban sections, principally of the metropolitan areas
options.B: The long-distance Mail and Express trains only
options.C: The trains run exclusively for the carriage of mails
options.D: The departmental and material trains run by the railway

e: Suburban earnings relate to local commuter services like EMU and local trains on notified suburban sections, principally of metropolitan areas, as against non-suburban earnings.

q: At a goods shed, a consignee's cart or truck loaded with goods taken delivery of is allowed to leave the station premises only on production of a gate pass, which serves mainly to show that:

options.A: The wagon in which the goods arrived has been released for reloading
options.B: Delivery of the goods has been duly granted and the freight and other charges due on the consignment have been paid or accounted for
options.C: The goods have been weighed again at the gate at the request of the consignee
options.D: The consignee has registered a claim for the goods at the destination station

e: A gate pass lets a consignee's vehicle leave the station only after showing delivery was duly granted and freight and other charges due were paid or accounted for.

q: A 'shortage certificate' issued by the destination station in respect of a consignment serves mainly as:

options.A: A receipt for the freight collected at the destination station
options.B: An authority for the consignor to rebook the missing packages free of charge
options.C: A demand note for the demurrage due on the consignment
options.D: A record evidencing the quantity of the consignment which was short delivered, to support the party's claim for the portion not received

e: A shortage certificate records the quantity short delivered at destination and serves as evidence to support the party's claim for the portion of the consignment not received.

q: A consignor who wishes to have a consignment already booked stopped in transit or diverted to another station, before delivery is effected, can have his instructions carried out only where:

options.A: He surrenders the Railway Receipt and complies with the prescribed conditions, including payment of the charges due for the interception or diversion
options.B: He merely sends a telegram to the destination station, without surrendering any document
options.C: The consignee at the original destination raises no objection in writing
options.D: The goods clerk at the booking station certifies that the consignment has not been weighed

e: Interception or diversion in transit is allowed only if the consignor surrenders the Railway Receipt and complies with the prescribed conditions, including paying the charges due.

q: A 'Risk Note' in connection with the booking of a consignment is a document executed by the consignor mainly where:

options.A: The freight on the consignment is left unpaid at the time of booking
options.B: The consignment is booked for a station to which booking is temporarily restricted
options.C: The goods are tendered in a defective condition or in defective packing, or are booked at owner's risk, the note recording the basis on which the Railways accept them
options.D: The consignee desires delivery of the goods without production of the Railway Receipt

e: A Risk Note is executed where goods are in defective condition or defective packing, or are booked at owner's risk, recording the basis on which the Railways accept them.

q: Where a consignment does not comply with the prescribed conditions of packing for carriage by rail, the correct course at the booking station is to:

options.A: Refuse the consignment in every case, whatever its condition
options.B: Accept it only on the prescribed conditions, recording a clear remark about the defective packing or condition on the Forwarding Note and the Railway Receipt
options.C: Book it at railway risk without making any remark anywhere
options.D: Levy wharfage on it before booking and record the levy on the invoice alone

e: A consignment with defective packing is accepted only on the prescribed conditions, with a clear remark about the defective packing or condition on the Forwarding Note and Railway Receipt.

q: Packages containing dangerous goods accepted for carriage by rail are required to be distinctly marked and labelled in the prescribed manner mainly in order to:

options.A: Enable the goods to be charged at the highest class rate in every case
options.B: Exempt the consignment from weighment at the booking station
options.C: Permit the goods to be carried in a passenger train as luggage
options.D: Warn the staff handling them of the dangerous nature of the contents, so that they are handled, loaded and carried with the precautions prescribed for such goods

e: Dangerous goods packages are distinctly marked and labelled to warn handling staff of their dangerous nature, so they are handled and carried with the prescribed precautions.

q: Articles of special value, such as gold, silver, currency notes and valuables, are accepted for carriage by rail only where:

options.A: Their nature and value are properly declared by the consignor and the special conditions prescribed for the booking of such articles are complied with
options.B: They are packed in an ordinary parcel wrapper without any declaration
options.C: The station master personally guarantees their safe carriage to destination
options.D: They are booked as ordinary luggage of the accompanying passenger

e: Articles of special value like gold, silver and currency notes are accepted only where their nature and value are properly declared and the special booking conditions are complied with.

q: For goods traffic moving under the Goods and Services Tax regime, the documents relating to the movement of the goods, such as the e-way bill where one is required, are primarily the responsibility of:

options.A: The Travelling Inspector of Accounts of the section
options.B: The destination station, which prepares them after the goods arrive
options.C: The consignor or the party causing the movement of the goods, the Railways carrying the consignment on the documents produced at booking
options.D: The Traffic Accounts Office, which issues them along with the Advice of Internal Check

e: Under GST, movement documents like the e-way bill are the responsibility of the consignor or party causing the movement; the Railways carry the goods on documents produced at booking.

q: Under Section 106 of the Railways Act, 1989, a person is not entitled to compensation for loss, destruction, damage or non-delivery of a consignment unless his claim to the compensation has been preferred in writing to the railway administration:

options.A: Within one month of the date of delivery of the consignment
options.B: Within three years of the date on which the goods were entrusted to the Railways
options.C: At any time, since no period is prescribed for preferring such a claim
options.D: Within six months from the date on which the goods were entrusted to the railway administration for carriage

e: Section 106 of the Railways Act bars compensation unless the claim is preferred in writing within six months from the date the goods were entrusted to the Railways for carriage.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Compensation under Section 124A of the Railways Act, 1989 is not payable where the death or injury of a passenger is due to suicide, attempted suicide or a self-inflicted injury.
2. Compensation under that section is also not payable where the death or injury is due to the passenger's own criminal act or an act committed in a state of intoxication or insanity.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: Both 1 and 2
options.B: 1 only
options.C: 2 only
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Section 124A excludes compensation where death or injury is due to suicide, attempted suicide or self-inflicted injury, and also for the passenger's own criminal act, intoxication or insanity.
